nameStory: The forget-me-not gets its romantic name from European folklore, where lovers would give these tiny blue flowers as a promise to remember each other always. The scientific name Myosotis literally means 'mouse ear' in Greek, referring to the small, soft, oval leaves that reminded early botanists of a mouse's fuzzy ears.
description: Field forget-me-not is a small, fuzzy annual or short-lived perennial plant that grows up to 16 inches tall with an upright, branching habit. Its most distinctive feature is clusters of tiny, sky-blue flowers that are only about 1/8 to 1/4 inch across, each with five rounded petals arranged in a perfect circle. The entire plant feels soft and slightly rough to the touch due to its covering of fine hairs. Originally from Europe, it has naturalized throughout New England in disturbed soils and open areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny grey-blue to sky-blue flowers, only 3-5mm across, shaped like perfect little saucers with five rounded petals and a yellow center. They grow in curled clusters that slowly unfurl as new buds open.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves that feel soft and fuzzy like velvet, arranged alternately along the stem. They're widest near the tip and taper toward the base, resembling tiny mouse ears.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright plant reaching 6-16 inches tall with multiple branching stems. The whole plant feels slightly rough and hairy when you brush against it, with hairs sticking out at right angles from the stems.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces clusters of tiny, dark brown, shiny nutlets that look like miniature coffee beans. Each flower develops into four small, hard seeds.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Covered in patent hairs that stick out perpendicular to the stem surface, giving it a distinctly fuzzy, almost bristly texture when touched.

habitat: Field forget-me-not thrives in open, disturbed areas with well-drained soil throughout New England. Look for it in farm fields, roadsides, vacant lots, garden edges, and anywhere the soil has been recently disturbed. It prefers sunny to partially shaded locations and often grows alongside other weedy species like dandelions and plantains.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin flowering in late spring, with the characteristic blue blooms appearing in small, coiled clusters that gradually unfurl.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with abundant tiny blue flowers. Seeds begin forming and ripening to dark brown by mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Annual plants complete their life cycle and die back, while short-lived perennials may persist. Seeds are dispersed and will germinate the following spring.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants are completely absent, existing only as seeds in the soil. Occasional short-lived perennial plants may survive as small basal rosettes under snow cover.

funFact: Forget-me-nots have one of the most ingenious pollination strategies in the plant world - their flower clusters are coiled like a fiddlehead fern and slowly unfurl over many days, ensuring there's always a fresh flower ready for pollinators while older flowers are already developing seeds!
confusionNotes: Field forget-me-not can be confused with other forget-me-not species, but it's distinguished by its annual growth habit, patent hairs on stems (sticking straight out), and preference for dry, disturbed soil rather than wet areas. Remember: 'field' forget-me-not likes 'dry fields,' while water forget-me-not prefers wet spots.
contextualKnowledge: Many gardeners are familiar with the cultivated wood forget-me-not sold in garden centers, but field forget-me-not is the scrappy wild cousin that shows up uninvited in disturbed soil. While considered a weed by some, it's actually quite beneficial as an early nectar source for small pollinators when few other flowers are available.
compareHints: Field forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring dry, disturbed soil rather than wet areas, and having more pronounced patent hairs on its stems. Unlike the perennial wood forget-me-not commonly sold in gardens, field forget-me-not is usually annual and has smaller flowers. It's also more tolerant of poor, compacted soils than its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Water forget-me-not is distinguished from other forget-me-not species by its preference for wet habitats and its perennial, mat-forming growth habit.
Blue forget-me-not is the most rigid and unbranched of all New England forget-me-nots, with distinctly smaller flowers than its relatives.
Wood forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring drier woodland soils versus wet areas, and it has a more compact growth habit.
Unlike the common water forget-me-not which stays bright blue and grows in wet areas, changing forget-me-not prefers drier disturbed soil and shows its telltale color progression.
Among New England's forget-me-nots, bay forget-me-not stands out for having the smallest flowers and most relaxed growth habit.
Among New England's forget-me-nots, early forget-me-not is the smallest and most easily overlooked.
